set.t: The Hinton St Mary Mosaic (Christian Panel with Bust of Christ and Chi-Rho)
set.c: Hinton St Mary, Dorset, Roman Britain (attributed to the Durnovaria/Dorchester workshop)
set.l: British Museum, London (central roundel on display; rest in storage)

summary: At the heart of this great Roman floor a roundel frames the bust of a clean-shaven man with intent dark eyes, his head set before the Chi-Rho, the monogram of Christ, and flanked by two pomegranates. Around him four lunettes show hounds chasing deer among trees, and in the corners four busts look inward. Laid in a Dorset house in the 4th century, it is one of the earliest surviving images of Christ in Britain and possibly the only one in an ancient pavement.
facts: The mosaic was discovered on 12 September 1963 by the local blacksmith, Walter John White, and lifted for the British Museum.

Most scholars identify the bust as Christ because of the Chi-Rho behind it, though the Emperor Constantine has also been proposed; the panel in the adjoining smaller room shows Bellerophon killing the Chimera.
It was chosen as Object 44 in the BBC Radio 4 series 'A History of the World in 100 Objects'.
notes: Dated on stylistic grounds to the 4th century (Wikipedia); excavations found nothing earlier than c. 270. The mosaic was lifted again and broken up in 1997, and only the central roundel is now displayed.

set.t: The Vision of Christ in Glory ('Icon of Christ of Latomos'), Apse Mosaic, Hosios David, Thessaloniki
set.l: Church of Hosios David (katholikon of the Latomos Monastery), Thessaloniki, Greece (in situ, apse)

summary: In the small apse of the Latomos monastery church a young, beardless Christ sits on a rainbow within a radiant circle of light, raising his right hand and holding an open scroll. The four winged creatures of Ezekiel's and John's visions emerge around the aureole, and below, the four rivers of Paradise flow from a rocky mount. Two prophets — usually identified as Ezekiel and Habakkuk — witness the vision, one in awe and one meditating over a book: a rare early image of the Lord revealed in glory.
facts: Christ's scroll carries a Greek text from Isaiah 25:9: 'Behold our God, in whom we hope and rejoice in our salvation, he will give rest to this house.'

According to a 12th-century account by Abbot Ignatius, the long-hidden image was revealed to the Egyptian monk Sennuphius when its covering of plaster fell away during an earthquake; the mosaic was rediscovered in the 1920s after the mosque was reconsecrated as a church.

Andreas Xyngopoulos dated the mosaic to the last quarter of the 5th century, a date generally accepted; the church is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments of Thessaloniki.

links.label: Wikipedia: Icon of Christ of Latomos

notes: The identity of the two witnesses is debated (Ezekiel and Habakkuk is the most widely held view; Grabar proposed Peter and Paul).

set.t: Ivory Plaque with the Crucifixion
set.l: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (17.190.495a)

summary: On this tiny plaque, barely four centimetres high, Christ hangs on the cross with arms outstretched along the beam, his head inclined and nimbed, wearing a long knotted loincloth, his feet resting on a small mound. Two haloed mourners — presumably the Virgin and St John — stand beneath the arms of the cross, each raising a hand to the cheek in grief, while two angels lean over the crossbeam above. Traces of gilding remain on the haloes.
facts: The Met dates the plaque to about 1000 (995–1005) and classes it as Ottonian; it measures only 4.1 × 2.8 cm.
It was given to the Metropolitan Museum by J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.
The gesture of hand to cheek is a long-established sign of mourning in Crucifixion imagery of this period.

notes: The Met's date of c. 1000 sits on the boundary of the early period. Which mourner is the Virgin and which John cannot be confirmed from the small photograph.

set.t: Statuette of the Good Shepherd
set.c: Probably Thessaloniki or the eastern Mediterranean
set.l: Museum of Byzantine Culture, Thessaloniki, Greece

summary: A youthful shepherd with a cap of curls stands on a small base, carrying a ram across his shoulders and steadying its legs with his right hand. He wears a belted short tunic and leggings, and a further animal lies at his feet; a supporting pillar rises behind him, and his left forearm is broken away. Small statuettes like this one turned the familiar pastoral figure into an image of Christ, who lays down his life for his sheep.
facts: The Museum of Byzantine Culture labels the statuette 'The Good Shepherd' and dates it to the 4th century (a photograph of the label reads 'second decade of the 4th century'; another source says mid-4th century).
Freestanding Good Shepherd statuettes are among the earliest Christian sculptures in the round; the type adapts the classical calf- or ram-bearer (kriophoros).

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Statuette of the Good Shepherd, Museum of Byzantine Culture

notes: Precise dating within the 4th century differs between sources. Medium (marble) is identified from photographs. As with all early Good Shepherd statuettes, the Christian reading rests on context and the museum's identification.

set.t: Christ Healing the Gerasene Demoniac (Sant'Apollinare Nuovo)
set.l: Basilica of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna (in situ, upper register of the nave)

summary: Against the gold ground the young, beardless Christ, robed in purple with a jewelled cross-nimbus, stretches out his hand towards the possessed man who crouches before a rocky outcrop, while a disciple in white raises his hand in witness. To the right, the swine into which the unclean spirits were sent plunge down into the blue water. With a handful of figures the mosaicist tells the whole story of Christ's authority over the powers of evil.
facts: It is one of the thirteen miracle and teaching scenes in the topmost register of the nave, made under Theodoric in the early 6th century; in all of them Christ appears young and beardless.
Three of the swine are shown in the water, a compact visual shorthand for the herd of the Gospel account.

set.t: The Virgin and Child in a Niche (Tokalı Kilise, Göreme)
set.l: Tokalı Kilise, Göreme Open-Air Museum, Nevşehir, Turkey (in situ)

summary: Within a shallow arched niche, lit against the rough tufa of the rock-cut church, the Virgin in a dark maphorion bends her head towards the Christ Child, who sits on her arm in an ochre garment and presses his face close to hers; both wear golden haloes, and the dark blue ground is scattered with small white stars. Above and around the niche the deep blue paintings of the New Church can be glimpsed. The tender, cheek-to-cheek embrace belongs to the Byzantine type of the Virgin of tenderness (Eleousa).
facts: Tokalı Kilise, the largest church at Göreme, consists of an Old Church of the early 10th century and a larger New Church added later in the century, whose paintings use costly lapis-lazuli blue.
An inscription names the painter of the New Church as Nikephoros and its patrons as Constantine and his son Leon.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Frescos in the Tokalı Kilise

notes: Commons descriptions (two independent photographers) date this niche painting to the 10th century; the Princeton Index of Medieval Art records an Eleousa Virgin and Child on the sanctuary east wall. Its exact phase (New Church c. 950–970, or later) is not confirmed; the New Church itself is dated variously from c. 960 to the end of the 10th or early 11th century.

set.t: Christ Enthroned between Saints Peter and Paul (Throne Wall Mosaic, Cappella Palatina, Palermo)

notes: The frieze above the mosaic, read from the photograph, is inscribed ANNO DOMINI MCCCCLXXVIII (1478), with heraldic shields; the throne-wall mosaic of Christ between Peter and Paul thus belongs at least in its present form to a late-15th-century remaking of the Norman decoration (chapel mosaics begun 1140s).
